verifyByViolation.method: git stash (removes the fix, restoring origin/main's exact pre-fix code) against the SAME running Postgres and seed data, re-run the identical curl requests, then git stash pop and re-verify the fix closes what the stash run showed.
verifyByViolation.confoundFoundAndCorrected: First attempt reused a still-running FIXED server on the same port (kill target was from a different shell process, job control does not cross Bash tool calls) -- caught because the 'violation' run returned 403, the FIXED behavior, which should have been a red flag on its own rather than accepted at face value. Found the real PID via Get-NetTCPConnection, killed it, and re-ran the old code cleanly before trusting any result. Recorded here per ENFORCEMENT.md's 'a convenient result is a reason to distrust the instrument, not a result.'
confirmedPreFixViolations: Anonymous read of a tenant folder list returns 401 pre-fix (WDLL requires 403) -- status-code gap real, not assumed.

The ONE shared token (ci-round-trip-token, no relationship to acme) reads acme's private folder list AND acme's private blob bytes verbatim ('tenant acme unchanged'), status 200, zero scope check -- the actual defect, reproduced against real data, not inferred from reading the code alone.
confirmedPostFixCloses: The identical anonymous request now returns 403.
The identical acme-blob-read-via-shared-token request, when attempted with a template-city-scoped token instead, now returns 403 with body {"error":"forbidden",...}.

The SAME shared token, now explicitly configured with a blanket ('*','*') grant, still succeeds for both template-city and acme reads -- proving the fix does not regress the already-deployed multi-tenant CI/backend pattern, only closes it for callers that are NOT holding that grant.

adversarialReviewOfOwnDesign: Question: does granting the legacy token a blanket '*'/'*' scope just keep the defect under a new name? Answer: no -- the defect was 'no caller identity is checked at all, ever, for any token'. Post-fix, an UNKNOWN or MISSING token always refuses; a KNOWN token's access is exactly what its grants say, and the blanket grant is an explicit, visible, single line of configuration a reviewer can see and revoke, not a code-level default. This is declared in the README and PR description, not left implicit.

Question: could the entityId-parse-fails case (malformed entityId) be exploited to bypass the scope check? Answer: no -- requireReadScope with an empty scopePairs array only succeeds for a caller holding the blanket grant (identityHasBlanketGrant short-circuits); a narrowly-scoped caller gets 403 on an unparseable id, never a free pass. Covered by the identityAllowsAnyScope unit test asserting exactly this.

Question: does the blob-scope lookup (getBlobScopes) correctly refuse an orphaned blob (bytes in smart_file_blobs with no citing version)? Answer: yes -- an orphan returns an empty scope-pair array, which only a blanket-grant caller can read, per the same fail-closed rule above.
